commitments: Account 7400 inventory shrink adjustment rose $62,300, from $8,900 to $71,200, which is 700.0 percent and is starred as passing both legs, and not one sentence in the memo mentions it. It is the largest unexplained movement in the pack.

Account 6100 fleet fuel: S9 says it declined $31,600, but the table shows $91,200 rising to $122,800, up $31,600 and 34.6 percent. The direction is reversed and diesel coming off a June peak cannot explain a 34.6 percent increase.

Account 6400 bad debt expense: S3 says a reduction of $84,700, but the movement is $62,000 down to $9,500, which is $52,500. The 84.7 is the percentage written in as if it were dollars, and releasing the Coastal Grocers reserve one month after taking it needs a cash receipt or a credit event behind it.
Account 6000 warehouse wages: S4 says wages rose $74,900, but $702,500 to $781,900 is $79,400. The digits are transposed and $4,500 of the movement is unaccounted for.

Account 5000 cost of product sold: S5 credits renegotiated inbound freight rates for the decline, but the note above the table says inbound freight is excluded from cost of product sold and sits on its own line. The driver is attached to the wrong account.

Account 5100 inbound freight fell $43,500 or 15.1 percent and is starred, yet the only sentence in the memo about freight rates is written against account 5000. The line that actually moved is left without a driver of its own.

Account 6200 repairs and maintenance: S10 says the depot repair program closed in June with no further repair spend expected this year, and S11 says the July repairs of $36,400 are the second phase of the dock program at Southline. Both sentences cannot be true.

Account 6800 marketing and trade shows: S2 says the $96,400 relates to a regional trade show in September. Cost for a September show is not July expense, so the $74,400 movement should be sitting in prepaid and released when the show runs.

Account 6500 professional fees: S12 defers a July interim review invoice of roughly $12,800 into August and calls that normal practice. July fieldwork belongs in July and should be accrued at close, and the $12,800 appears nowhere in the table.

Account 4000 distribution revenue: S6 explains the $214,000 decline as a seasonal slowdown, while S8 discloses that customer freight billings were reclassified into distribution revenue in June. June is inflated by that reclassification, so the month on month comparison is not like for like and the seasonal driver has not been tested against it.

Account 6600 utilities: a $3,300 movement at 6.0 percent fails both legs of the threshold and gets the longest sentence in the memo, covering a tariff re rating, chiller load and the other two depots, while account 7400 at $62,300 gets nothing.
Account 4100 service revenue: S1 writes commentary on a 5.3 percent movement that fails the percentage leg, which is more space spent on a line that required none.

Account 4000 distribution revenue: S6 leans on a comparison to the same month last year, and no prior year figure appears anywhere in this pack, so the assertion cannot be tested by anyone reading the memo.
aided_findings: Account 6400 bad debt expense: beyond the amount error, the Coastal Grocers reserve was taken one month ago and is now released in full with no cash receipt, settlement or credit event named. A reserve that goes on and comes off inside two closes is a judgement I would want papered before release.

Account 4000 distribution revenue: the challenge list tested S6 for support but never connected it to S8. The June reclassification of freight billings into distribution revenue inflates the June base, so part of the $214,000 decline is the reclassification unwinding rather than school nutrition seasonality.

C1.reason: Utilities moved $3,300 on $54,900, which is 6.0 percent, so it fails both legs and no commentary is owed. S7 is the longest sentence in the memo, running through a tariff re rating and chiller load, and it displaced account 7400 at $62,300 and 700 percent, which got nothing.

C2.reason: The fieldwork was performed in July, so the cost belongs in July and should have been accrued at close, debit professional fees and credit accrued liabilities for the $12,800. Calling the deferral normal practice makes it a standing policy error rather than a one month slip.

C3.reason: May is not in this comparison, so the $214,000 cited cannot be tied to anything in the pack. The inference is also backwards: inbound freight fell $43,500 and 15.1 percent from June to July, which is what a July 1 rate change would look like, not evidence that it failed to take effect.

C4.reason: The note above the table says inbound freight is excluded from cost of product sold and sits on its own line, so a freight rate change cannot drive the $147,000 decline in account 5000. It explains account 5100, and the $147,000 in cost of product sold is left with no driver at all.

C5.reason: The account moved $702,500 to $781,900, which is $79,400, and S4 says $74,900. The digits are transposed, $4,500 is unaccounted for, and the overtime story is being offered for a number the memo did not actually compute.

C6.reason: The spend supports a trade show that runs in September, so it belongs in September. It should have been posted to prepaid expense in July and released to marketing when the show takes place, which means the $74,400 movement in July expense should not be there.

C7.reason: I have seen nothing supporting the school nutrition seasonality, and the comparison to the same month last year rests on prior year figures that appear nowhere in this pack. I would want revenue by customer segment for both months and the actual prior July before anyone relies on that sentence.

C8.reason: Shrink moved $8,900 to $71,200, which is $62,300 and 700.0 percent, clearing both legs several times over, and no sentence mentions it. I would want the cycle count results, the write off detail by depot and the journal entries, particularly with warehouse wages up $79,400 on overtime in the same month.

C9.reason: The arithmetic is off by a factor of ten. $31,700 less $30,100 is $1,600, not $16,000, and $1,600 on $30,100 is 5.3 percent, not 53 percent. The line fails both legs of the threshold, so no seat count and no commentary are owed on it.

C10.reason: There is no transfer to find between these two. Account 4100 is revenue billed to customers for maintaining their equipment and account 6200 is expense on our own depots, so no entry debits one and credits the other. The amounts do not correspond either, $55,000 against $82,200, and account 4100 at 5.3 percent fails the threshold anyway.

C11.reason: The reclassification matters more than the $7,500. If customer freight billings were moved into distribution revenue during June, then the June base for both account 4200 and account 4000 is distorted and this month on month comparison is not like for like, which is exactly what S6 leans on when it calls the revenue decline seasonal.

C12.reason: The movement is $62,000 down to $9,500, which is $52,500, and the sentence says $84,700. That figure is the 84.7 percent decline written back in as dollars, so the memo has turned a percentage into a currency amount and overstated the release by $32,200.

C13.reason: The table shows $91,200 rising to $122,800, up $31,600 and 34.6 percent, and S9 says it declined by that same figure. The sign is reversed, and diesel coming off a June peak is the opposite of what a 34.6 percent increase in fuel cost shows.

C14.reason: S10 says the depot repair program closed in June with no further repair spend expected this year and S11 says the July repairs are the second phase of the dock program at Southline. I believe S11 because $36,400 was actually spent, and it matters because the close needs an accrual for whatever remains committed on that program.
